en.name: Eucharistic Vision of Liege
en.summary: Recurring visions reported by a thirteenth-century Belgian nun of a moon with a dark gap led directly to the local, and later universal, institution of the Feast of Corpus Christi.
en.body: Juliana of Liege, a nun and later prioress at a convent near Liege, in present-day Belgium, reported recurring visions from a young age of a bright full moon marked by one dark gap, which she came to understand, after years of prayerful reflection, as representing the absence from the Church's calendar of a feast specifically dedicated to honoring the Blessed Sacrament, distinct from its commemoration within Holy Thursday's larger Passion-focused liturgy. Despite considerable resistance and personal hardship, including exile from her own convent, she persisted in promoting the idea, and the local bishop of Liege instituted a diocesan feast of Corpus Christi in 1246 on her recommendation. This local feast provided the direct template that Pope Urban IV, prompted separately by the Eucharistic miracle at Bolsena-Orvieto, extended to the entire Church less than two decades later, making Juliana's visions and advocacy the originating impulse behind what became one of Catholicism's major universal feasts.
